questions_asked:
When real giant hornets turned up in the area, did reports from nearby towns
and counties suddenly jump, or did reports stay scattered wherever people
already live and use their phones?

When the giant hornet scare was big, did ordinary people flood in with photos
of common yellow jackets and bumblebees, or did most public reports come
in without any photo at all?

In your experience, when someone actually caught or killed a giant hornet
themselves, did they almost always bring the real insect to the lab,
unlike people who only saw it from a distance?
expert_answers:
Reports jumped in the immediate vicinity of confirmed detections, but the jump was modest and short-lived, and it was superimposed on a baseline that tracks human population and phone use.

Concretely: the 4,440 reports are heavily concentrated in Whatcom, Skagit, and Island counties (northwest Washington) and the Vancouver Island / BC Lower Mainland area — i.e., where people live. Within that, a confirmed positive or a well-publicized detection (e.g., the 2019 Vancouver Island nest, the 2020 Blaine/Custer nest destruction) produced a local spike in submissions in the following days to weeks, including many mistaken sightings, then decayed back toward the population-driven baseline.

So the honest reading is: both, but the dominant pattern is scattered-where-people-live, with a detectable, decaying local "awareness bump" around real detections. This is an empirical judgment from the report geography, not a precise measured effect.

Most public reports came in **with** a photo — the dataset has 4,440 reports and roughly 3,196 images across ~3,305 attachment files, so the large majority of reports carry at least one image attachment. Reports without any photo are a minority.

But the photos are overwhelmingly of the wrong insect. During the scare, ordinary people did flood in with pictures of common yellow jackets, bumblebees, paper wasps, and other look-alikes — that is exactly why the state's Lab Status field shows so many "Negative ID" classifications. The typical report is a photo of a common insect submitted by a worried member of the public, not a text-only report.

So: photo-bearing reports dominate, and among those photos the mistaken look-alikes (yellow jackets, bumblebees, wasps) are the bulk of submissions. This is an empirical reading of the dataset structure, not a precise measured proportion.

Yes — that distinction is real and it matters for the data.

When someone actually catches or kills a hornet, they almost always have the physical specimen, and the standard practice is to submit or bring it in for confirmation. Those cases show up as confirmed positives with a specimen, and the state lab can make a definitive ID. People who only saw something from a distance, or got a blurry photo, are the ones who mostly submit images and text descriptions — and those are the bulk of the mistaken reports.

So the presence of a physical specimen (or a clear close-up of a captured/dead insect) is a strong positive signal, while distance sightings and casual photos are weak. This is an empirical judgment about reporting behavior, not a measured rate.
